tldr: We propose a two-stage framework that generates kinematically feasible whole-body references online via reduced-order reinforcement learning combining single rigid body dynamics with full humanoid kinematics, and tracks them using a whole-body policy. On a real Unitree G1 robot, a single unified policy achieves backward speeds of -2.0 m/s to forward speeds of 2.8 m/s, turning at ±3.0 rad/s, one-legged hopping, and rough-terrain traversal with smooth continuous transitions.
hero_caption: Overview of FORGE. Based on high-level velocity or hopping commands, a reduced-order model (ROM) policy generates whole-body reference trajectories online, which a low-level full-order model (FOM) tracking policy then executes on the robot as joint commands.
overview:
Achieving agile and versatile locomotion on humanoid robots is one of the grand challenges in robotics. Humanoids are high-dimensional, nonlinear, underactuated systems governed by hybrid dynamics with switching ground contacts. Classical optimization-based approaches like model predictive control (MPC) face a dilemma: solving the full-order dynamics model (FOM) online is computationally intractable for real-time rates, while relying on simplified reduced-order models (ROMs) like point masses ignores joint limits and limb inertia, often leading to tracking failure on hardware. On the other hand, recent deep reinforcement learning (RL) can train robust controllers, but typically depends on human motion capture data or requires switching between separate policies tailored to specific tasks or speed regimes.

To address this, the authors propose "FORGE", a two-stage learning framework that elegantly combines the strengths of both worlds. In the first stage, they build a lightweight custom simulator pairing single rigid body (SRB) dynamics with the robot's full humanoid kinematics (IK) to train an online "ROM reference generator" that produces feasible whole-body trajectories across a broad command envelope in real time. In the second stage, a "whole-body tracking policy" is trained in a full-order dynamics simulator via imitation learning to track the trajectories streamed by this frozen ROM generator.

Demonstrated on the Unitree G1 humanoid hardware without any pre-computed motion libraries or motion capture data, this single unified policy achieves backward running at -2.0 m/s, sprinting up to 2.8 m/s (4.0 m/s in simulation), yaw turns at ±3.0 rad/s, lateral strafing at ±1.0 m/s, seamless transitions to one-legged hopping, and zero-shot deployment over outdoor grass slopes and deep sand.
contributions: Built a learning-based reference generator combining single rigid body (SRB) dynamics with full humanoid kinematics that generates dynamically and kinematically feasible whole-body trajectories online over a broad command space.
Established a two-stage reinforcement learning framework that couples an online ROM reference generator with whole-body tracking policy training in a full-order dynamics (FOM) environment.

Demonstrated on a real Unitree G1 humanoid that a single unified policy achieves longitudinal speeds from -2.0 to 2.8 m/s, angular velocities of ±3.0 rad/s, lateral speeds of ±1.0 m/s, one-legged hopping, and smooth continuous transitions across these commands zero-shot.

sections.heading: Why is whole-body agile humanoid locomotion so difficult?
sections.summary: Existing optimization-based trajectory generation and reinforcement learning suffer from trade-offs among compute cost, generality, and motion data acquisition costs. This paper proposes a two-stage framework coupling online reduced-order reference generation with whole-body tracking control to cover a broad command space using a single unified policy.
sections.details:
While humanoid robots have shown impressive individual dynamic motions, unifying them into a single control framework capable of agile and versatile movement remains exceptionally challenging. Humanoids have high degrees of freedom and are underactuated, nonlinear hybrid systems whose contact states constantly switch.

In classical model-based control, locomotion is typically decomposed into two layers: reference trajectory generation and whole-body tracking control. Optimizing trajectories over a full-order model (FOM) produces dynamically consistent motions, but the computational cost is prohibitive for online real-time planning. Conversely, reduced-order models (ROMs) that approximate the robot as a point mass or pendulum permit fast online solving, but neglecting joint limits, limb ranges of motion, and leg inertia often causes tracking failure when executed on hardware.

On the other hand, recent deep reinforcement learning (RL) leverages massive parallel simulation to synthesize robust controllers. However, mastering a wide velocity envelope and diverse locomotion gaits within a single policy remains difficult, often requiring policy-switching architectures. While imitation-based RL provides high-quality references to guide learning toward natural behaviors, relying on large-scale human motion capture (MoCap) datasets brings morphology mismatches and high collection costs.

To solve this, the authors introduce a novel two-stage framework: Stage 1 trains an online whole-body reference generator via RL in a custom simulator combining SRB dynamics with full kinematics, and Stage 2 trains a whole-body tracking policy in a full-order dynamics environment tracking the references streamed online from this generator. This allows a single unified policy to master an extraordinarily wide operating envelope without relying on any external datasets.

sections.heading: From reduced-order models to motion tracking: evolution and bottlenecks
sections.summary: We review classic reduced-order models such as linear inverted pendulums and their use in RL as reward shaping. We also highlight the limitations of existing motion-imitation tracking controllers that rely on human motion capture, framing the unique advantages of this work.
sections.details:
### II-A Lineage of Reduced-Order Models (ROMs) in Humanoid Locomotion
ROMs are powerful tools for abstracting complex humanoid physics into tractable representations. A prominent example is the linear inverted pendulum (LIP) model assuming constant center-of-mass height, alongside its variants: HLIP (accounting for hybrid contact transitions), ALIP (incorporating angular momentum about the stance foot), and SLIP (modeling leg spring compliance in the vertical axis). Expanding beyond these, the single rigid body (SRB) model captures both translational and rotational momentum dynamics. SRB models, coupled with foothold planners, have been widely used in model predictive control (MPC) to optimize ground reaction forces and moments (GRFM).

In RL, ROMs have also been utilized, but primarily as auxiliary reward guidance (e.g., target step lengths or angular momentum) or as offline pre-computed trajectory libraries. In contrast, this paper requires the ROM itself to satisfy full-body kinematic constraints and generate dynamic whole-body reference trajectories online.

### II-B Reference Trajectory Generation for Humanoids
In imitation-based RL, high-quality reference trajectories are crucial for stable training. Prior trajectory optimization approaches often rely on static offline libraries, which struggle with smooth transitions across dynamic commands. Meanwhile, retargeting human motion data to humanoids frequently leads to dynamically infeasible references due to kinematic and mass distribution mismatches. Generating diverse reference motions on-the-fly for varied downstream tasks remains an open problem.

### II-C Whole-Body Motion Tracking
For tracking reference motions on physical robots, imitation-based RL has demonstrated compelling results, spanning physics-based character animation to real-world humanoid teleoperation. Recent architectures explore hierarchical setups using diffusion models as high-level motion generators followed by low-level tracking policies. However, these systems inherently rely on extensive human MoCap datasets, constrained by data collection overhead and hardware morphology mismatches. This work circumvents that dependence by self-generating references entirely through physics-based ROM reinforcement learning.

In Stage 2 (right), the frozen ROM generator is rolled out online to train a whole-body tracking policy in a full-order dynamics (FOM) simulator.

sections.heading: Fundamentals: Single rigid body dynamics and POMDP formulation
sections.summary: We formulate the Newton-Euler equations governing single rigid body (SRB) dynamics, the foundation of this work. We also describe the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) framework used for reinforcement learning under real-world sensing uncertainties.
sections.details:
### III-A Single Rigid Body (SRB) Dynamics
The SRB model assumes that the robot's limbs are massless, lumping the total mass and moment of inertia into a single rigid body around the center of mass of the floating base. This allows the translational and rotational dynamics of the floating base to be compactly expressed via Newton-Euler equations:
$$\begin{bmatrix} \dot{\mathbf{v}}_{\textnormal{B}} \\ \dot{\bm{\omega}}_{\textnormal{B}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{G} \\ -\mathbf{I}_{\textnormal{B}}^{-1} (\bm{\omega}_{\textnormal{B}} \times \mathbf{I}_{\textnormal{B}} \bm{\omega}_{\textnormal{B}}) \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{m}\mathbf{I}_{3\times 3} & \mathbf{0}_{3\times 3} \\ \mathbf{0}_{3\times 3} & \mathbf{I}_{\textnormal{B}}^{-1} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{F} \\ \mathbf{M} \end{bmatrix}$$
where $\mathbf{v}_{\textnormal{B}}, \bm{\omega}_{\textnormal{B}} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ are the linear and angular velocities of the base, $\mathbf{G} = [0, 0, -g]^\top$ is the gravity vector, $m$ is the total mass, and $\mathbf{I}_{\textnormal{B}}$ is the inertia tensor. The external net force $\mathbf{F}$ and moment $\mathbf{M}$ are computed by summing the ground reaction forces and moments (GRFM) applied across the left and right feet during contact.

### III-B Reinforcement Learning and POMDPs
Humanoid control is framed as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), as onboard proprioceptive sensors provide incomplete and noisy measurements of the true environment state $\mathbf{s}_t$. Because a single observation cannot fully identify the system state, the policy $\pi$ outputs action $\mathbf{a}_t$ conditioned on a history of past observations $\mathbf{o}_{t-h:t}$, past actions $\mathbf{a}_{t-h-1:t-1}$, and user command inputs $\mathbf{o}_{\textnormal{cmd}}$.

sections.heading: [Stage 1] Training a kinematically constrained ROM reference generator
sections.summary: A dedicated ROM simulator was built to couple SRB dynamics with real-time full-body inverse kinematics. By incorporating contact modes, gait phase variables, and a mix of task, gait shaping, and torque regularization rewards, the generator learns high-quality, feasible reference motions.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Custom ROM Simulator Environment
The primary reason pure ROM trajectories fail on real robots is that they ignore kinematic constraints such as joint limits and velocity bounds. To overcome this without running a heavy full-physics engine, the authors developed a custom numerical ROM simulator:
- **Coupling Dynamics with Kinematics**: Only the floating base is integrated via SRB dynamics, while end-effectors (feet and hands) are driven kinematically via task-space accelerations. At each time step, inverse kinematics (IK) is solved from the base pose and end-effector positions to recover full-order joint positions $\mathbf{q}_{\textnormal{FOM}}$. Although limbs are assumed massless, stance leg joint torques $\bm{\tau}_{\textnormal{legs}}$ are approximated via the contact Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{\textnormal{c}}$ as $\bm{\tau}_{\textnormal{legs}} = \mathbf{J}_{\textnormal{c}}^\top \bm{\lambda}_{\textnormal{F}}$.
- **Foot Contact Kinematics**: Each foot features 4 contact points (two at the heel, two at the toe). Foot roll is constrained to zero to prevent slippage and unnatural edge contacts, while pitch rotations about the heel or toe contact points are allowed.
- **Gait Phasing**: A normalized phase variable $\phi \in [0, 1)$ drives coordinated stepping, with the legs offset by 0.5. When the phase exceeds a liftoff threshold $\phi_{\textnormal{to}}$, the foot transitions to the swing phase.

### IV-C ROM MDP Formulation
The observation $\mathbf{o}_t^{\textnormal{ROM}}$ consists of base pose and velocity, end-effector poses and velocities, foot contact indicators, phase trigonometric encodings, velocity and hopping commands, and previous actions and stride history.
The action $\mathbf{a}_t^{\textnormal{ROM}}$ is 28-dimensional: end-effector task-space accelerations, foot pitch/yaw angles, desired GRFM for both feet (12 dimensions), gait period scaling factor $\alpha_T$, and liftoff threshold $\phi_{\textnormal{to}}$.

### IV-D Reward Function Design
The reward structure spans four main categories:
- **Task Rewards**: Gaussian kernel tracking of commanded velocities $(v_x^{\textnormal{cmd}}, v_y^{\textnormal{cmd}}, \omega_z^{\textnormal{cmd}})$, holding the highest weights.
- **Locomotion & Gait Timing Rewards**: Standing bonuses that encourage double support when velocity commands are near zero, along with penalties for deviating from the nominal gait period.
- **Gait Shaping Rewards**: Penalties on base posture tilt, foot orientation errors, and a reference tracking reward for speed-dependent arm swinging. Although arms are massless in the SRB model, generating coordinated arm swing trajectories dramatically stabilizes Stage 2 learning.
- **Regularization Rewards**: Normalized leg torque penalties to prevent excessive motor strain, using a sharp 6th-power penalty formulation near actuator limits.

sections.heading: [Stage 2] Tracking the online-generated references with full-order dynamics
sections.summary: The ROM generator trained in Stage 1 is frozen and deployed online within a full-order dynamics (FOM) environment. Built upon BeyondMimic, the whole-body tracking policy learns to track reference motions supplemented with ROM gait phase, command history, and dynamics-bridging tracking rewards.
sections.details:
In Stage 2, the whole-body tracking policy is trained in a high-fidelity physical simulator (FOM) matching the real robot hardware. The key design principle is that rather than replaying pre-recorded static trajectories, the Stage 1 ROM policy is frozen and rolled out online in real time, generating reference streams on the fly.

### Network Inputs and Observation Stacking
The tracking framework builds upon BeyondMimic, a robust imitation learning baseline. The observation $\mathbf{o}_t^{\textnormal{FOM}}$ extends standard BeyondMimic inputs (full kinematic reference, proprioception, past actions) by including phase information $\mathbf{o}_{\textnormal{phase}}$ and command inputs $\mathbf{o}_{\textnormal{cmd}}$ directly from the high-level ROM planner. Crucially, these ROM-derived features are stacked across the recent 3 steps ($H=3$). This enables the policy to anticipate the planner's immediate motion intent rather than viewing an isolated snapshot.

### Reward Design: Bridging the ROM-to-FOM Dynamics Gap
The reward extends BeyondMimic's tracking terms with essential additions. Because the ROM model assumes massless limbs, an inherent physical discrepancy exists between the ROM and FOM dynamics due to limb inertia and unmodeled ground contact mechanics. To compensate for this gap, a direct base twist tracking reward ($w_{\textnormal{twist}}=0.5$) is added to align FOM base velocity with the command. Furthermore, a 6th-power normalized leg torque penalty evaluated using FOM joint torques is introduced to ensure safe actuator limits during hardware deployment.

sections.heading: From 10+ km/h sprinting to one-legged hops and sand running under one policy
sections.summary: Both the ROM generator and whole-body tracker run synchronously online at 50 Hz, evaluated in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1. A single policy achieves -2.0 to 2.8 m/s longitudinal speeds, ±3.0 rad/s turning, strafing, one-legged hopping, and zero-shot transfer to slopes and sand.
sections.details:
### VI-A Simulation Evaluation: Unified High Speeds and Hopping
In simulation, the reference generator (ROM) and tracker (FOM) operate coupled online at 50 Hz. Under aggressive time-varying commands, the robot accelerated from 0 m/s to a 4.0 m/s sprint (14.4 km/h), reversed instantly into a -2.0 m/s backward run, and smoothly returned to a 1.0 m/s walk. As seen in Figure F4, the ROM reference promptly tracked commands, and the FOM model closely replicated the full-body kinematics. Furthermore, overlaying a "right leg hop" command while cruising forward at 1.0 m/s resulted in a seamless transition into single-legged hopping without destabilizing the robot.

### VI-B Hardware Experiments: Seamless Omnidirectional Maneuvers
On the physical Unitree G1 robot, commands were varied aggressively up to $\omega_z = \pm 3.0~\mathrm{rad/s}$ in yaw rate and $v_y = \pm 1.0~\mathrm{m/s}$ in lateral speed. Real-time IMU and odometry measurements closely matched the commands, handling zero-crossing directional reversals with high fluidity. Notably, no task-specific gain tuning or policy switching was used; the exact same unified network executed forward, backward, lateral, and in-place spinning motions continuously.

### VI-C Unstructured Real-World Environments and Peak Speed
Although trained exclusively on flat rigid terrain, the policy exhibited remarkable zero-shot robustness:
- **Sloped Grass**: The robot sprinted across outdoor uneven, slippery grass slopes without falling.
- **One-Legged Hopping on Sand**: Walking over soft, deformable sand, the robot smoothly transitioned into dynamic single-legged hopping and back to regular walking.
- **Hardware Top Speed**: Under a forward command of $v_x^{\textnormal{cmd}}=3.0~\mathrm{m/s}$, the robot achieved an average measured speed of approximately $2.8~\mathrm{m/s}$ (about 10.1 km/h) over a 15-foot course. While simulation reached 4.0 m/s, real-world execution was capped at 2.8 m/s due to actuator limits, demonstrating exceptional agility for a compact humanoid.

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: The FORGE framework couples ROM planning with whole-body RL tracking, mastering a broad velocity envelope and diverse locomotion behaviors in a single policy. Future work will investigate ablation studies, baseline comparisons, and theoretical tracking error analyses.
sections.details:
This work introduces a new control paradigm for agile and versatile humanoid locomotion. The core insight is training an online whole-body reference generator via ROM reinforcement learning that integrates single rigid body dynamics with kinematic constraints, directly driving a full-order tracking policy.

Hardware experiments on the Unitree G1 validate that a single unified policy can span longitudinal speeds from -2.0 to 2.8 m/s, lateral speeds up to ±1.0 m/s, yaw rates of ±3.0 rad/s, as well as one-legged hopping and rough-terrain adaptation.

For future directions, the authors plan to conduct detailed ablation studies assessing individual components (such as specific reward terms and observation stacking), perform quantitative benchmarking against existing MPC and end-to-end RL baselines, and pursue rigorous theoretical analyses of the tracking performance across the ROM-to-FOM dynamics gap.

takeaways: Integrating full-body inverse kinematics (IK) directly into reduced-order model (ROM) learning generates dynamically and kinematically feasible reference trajectories online without joint-limit violations.
Without relying on human motion capture data, a physics-based ROM reference generator can synthesize versatile, coordinated gaits with natural arm swings for walking, sprinting, and hopping.

Decoupling reference generation from full-order tracking while coupling them online enables a single unified neural policy to span wide speed envelopes and seamlessly transition between diverse locomotion gaits.
Policies trained entirely on flat terrain transfer zero-shot to challenging real-world surfaces like sloped grass and loose sand when guided by kinematically feasible whole-body references.
limitations: Because the ROM assumes massless limbs, high-speed leg swing motions create a wider dynamics discrepancy with the real full-order robot, increasing reliance on tracking correction rewards.

High-speed sprinting at 4.0 m/s and sustained single-legged hopping achieved in simulation could not be fully demonstrated on hardware due to physical motor torque and thermal limits of the Unitree G1.
Ablation studies isolating the impact of individual reward terms and architectural choices, as well as quantitative comparisons against state-of-the-art baselines, have not yet been fully conducted.
